To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the heritability explained in a genome-wide association study of type 2diabetes is largely due to genetic variants that are not genome-wide significant, and that expression quantitative trait locis identified in skeletal muscle, adipose, and lymphoblatoid cell lines account for a disproportionate amount of heritability.
eQTLs account for a disproportionate fraction of the genetic variance in T2D and that this fraction is greater in lean Hispanics and in adipose tissue.

The heritability of T2D is substantially greater than the proportion of phenotypes variance accounted for by genome wide-significant SNPs, but is explained by a smaller set of variants, identified as expression quantitative trait locis (eQTL) in human adipose, muscle and lymphoblast cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that genetic variation plays in human health.
the genetic component of type 2 Diabetes (T2D), which is a complex disease with a strong genetic basis.
the role of eQTLs as a source of genetic variation that influences complex traits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic variants associated with T2D are enriched in eQTLs identified across multiple tissues.
the heritability explained is greater than the proportion of variance explained by genome-wide significant SNPs.

eQTLs identified in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle explain a substantial portion of the heritabilities observed in the WTCCC and Starr County, Texas, data sets, but the contribution of eQTLs to the genetic component of the disease varies by ethnicity and body mass index.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cross-tissue e-QTLs account for a significant proportion of the heritabilities of T2D and related phenotypes.

the majority of the heritabilty for T2D can be explained by the additive effects of variants identified through GWAS, but that a substantial proportion of the heritablity for T2D is explained by variants that are not identified in GWAS.
eQTLs, particularly those that act across tissues, account for more of the genetic variance in T2D than do variants that are not eQTLs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic variation in the regulatory architecture that controls gene expression across tissues can account for a significant proportion of phenotypically relevant genetic variation.

the heritability explained for complex diseases is not evenly distributed among all genetic variants interrogated in GWASs; rather, it is concentrated among a subset of variants that are likely to be regulatory.
the genetic architecture underlying complex traits such as T2D is likely to be highly polygenic, with a substantial contribution from tissue-specific and cross-tissue eSNPs.
